newsitem.title: USA: Bombing defense suggests evidence contaminated.
newsitem.headline: Bombing defense suggests evidence contaminated.

text.p: The defence in the Oklahoma City bombing trial on Tuesday hammered away at an FBI scientist, suggesting that key evidence could have been contaminated because of sloppy handling and testing methods.

The cross-examination of FBI Special Agent Steven Burmeister was crucial because the FBI's Washington, D.C., laboratory has come under severe criticism in a recent Justice Department study that cited deficient operations.
Attorneys for accused bomber Timothy McVeigh were doing all they could to exploit the agency's documented weaknesses.

On Monday, Burmeister, who is acting head of the Chemical Toxicology Unit at the FBI lab, offered damaging testimony that traces of explosives were found on the clothes McVeigh was wearing when he was arrested soon after the April 19, 1995 bombing.

Explosives residue was also found on earplugs McVeigh had in his pocket and on a panel of the Ryder truck allegedly used in the bombing of the Alfred P. Murrah federal building that killed 168 people.
The prosecution's case is moving along at a rapid pace and the government could rest its case by Wednesday, a source close to the case said.

On Tuesday, defence attorney Christopher Tritico suggested that McVeigh's clothes and other evidence on which traces of explosives residue were found could have been contaminated during transportation or at different sections at the FBI lab.
"You don't know what, if any, contamination existed in the special photo unit?" Tritico asked.
Burmeister replied: "I have no reason to believe there was contamination of explosives there." But he conceded that no testing was done to establish if there was any contamination.

The defence has also suggested that McVeigh's clothes could have become contaminated at the Noble County prison in Perry, Oklahoma, where McVeigh was first held. Burmeister conceded that he made no attempt in May 1995 to find out whether anybody who had recently been jailed had handled explosives or if employees at the jail had been in contact with explosives.
Tritico also got Burmeister to admit that the FBI lab was updating its procedures for processing evidence in preparation for two inspections that will be made soon.
"Why are they inspecting the lab?" Tritico asked, prompting an objection from the prosecution, which the judge sustained.
Burmeister admitted that if evidence was improperly handled it could become contaminated at any step in the investigation.
He also conceded that evidence could become contaminated if investigators at the crime scene did not take precautions such as changing gloves, wearing protective clothings or using proper packaging.
But Burmeister said he had no direct knowledge that any of the evidence had not been properly packaged.

McVeigh's clothes were placed in a brown paper bag right after his arrest. Burmeister admitted that there are "better methods of transportation" to have carried McVeigh's clothes from the Oklahoma jail to the FBI lab in Washington.
Burmeister also conceded that the FBI did not test trucks and planes used to carry evidence beforehand to see if they were contaminated.
Burmeister admitted that no explosives residue was found in a storage shed near Herington, Kansas, that prosecutors claim was used to house the bomb's components.
Also, no explosives residue nor ammonium nitrate were found in McVeigh's 1977 Mercury Marquis, despite a vigorous search, Burmeister admitted.
McVeigh has pleaded not guilty and if convicted faces the death penalty.
